newsitem.title: UK: Balkans stand aside as East Europe prospers.
newsitem.headline: Balkans stand aside as East Europe prospers.

text.p: Unrest in the Balkans is making foreign investors even more apprehensive of a region whose economic and political mismanagement sets much of it apart from the rest of blossoming East Europe, analysts said on Tuesday.
There have been weeks of anti-government protests in Yugoslavia and Bulgaria, and the economies in both countries have been malfunctioning.
In Albania, the most impoverished of them all, troops have been used against protestors, enraged by the loss of their savings in pyramid investment schemes.

Unless there are radical changes, some Balkan countries can expect little of the foreign investment flooding into the rest of the former East Bloc as it switches to a market economy and a more democratic brand of politics, analysts warned.
"They are insider markets. Insider markets are never going to work," said Merrill Lynch analyst Andrew Kenningham.
Corruption is a crucial issue, with officials often more focused in trying to get what they can out of the existing economy than trying to turn it into something more productive, he said.
Analysts point to the communist past that dominates the ruling parties in Yugoslavia and Bulgaria and their distrust of the West and its demands for market reform.
In Bulgaria, president Peter Stoyanov is pressing the ruling Socialists to accept demands for early elections so that a new government can get on with the urgent task of introducing economic reform.
So precarious is the government's reputation that rumours on Tuesday it had failed to make a payment to service its foreign debt immediately knocked down the price of its Brady bonds.
The government later said it had met the payments.
But until Bulgaria can get agreement with the International Monetary Fund, analysts warn that default remains a real possibility.
The IMF is refusing to do a deal on lending Bulgaria money until the country has a stable government.
"Even if they form a new government, it is still going to be difficult to meet their obligations for the rest of this year," Rob van de Wijngaert, analyst with ABN-AMRO, cautioned.

Yugoslavia's situation is even worse in the eys of most analysts who say the government of Slobodan Milosevic threw away any opportunity to get early financial help from the West when he annulled opposition victories in local elections last November.

"The government missed their chance, they missed everything. We're still not there, but we're not far (from economic collapse)," said one banker close to negotiations to reschedule Yugoslavia's foreign commercial debt.

"We are getting very worried. Are they ready for democracy? Up to now it has been an "I look after myself first" mentality. If everyone does that, some people get rich and the country goes down and down," the banker said.
The riots in Albania too can only undermine efforts to build up the economy, analysts said.
"In Albania, there is a genuine desire to see progress but it does require a superhuman effort to get there," joint head of project finance at Charterhouse, Adam Seymour, said.
"This (latest unrest) won't help," he said, adding the international criticism over the treatment of the opposition in elections last year had taken already taken some of the shine off the country.
But there are some brighter hopes in the region, including Romania where a new government has pledged to liberalise the economy.
Among the group of former Yugoslavia republics, many analysts are looking at Slovenia, and probably Croatia, as firm candidates for sound economic growth and foreign investment.
"Perhaps what they (the countries falling behind) need is a really big bang," one banker said.
"Look at those demonstrators in Yugoslavia. They have such brilliant ideas. A lot of that sort of imagination in business there would be just wonderful," she added.
